claim: CaBP2 is highly abundant in inner hair cells (IHCs).
source: Besides CaBP2, the structurally related CaBP1 is highly abundant in the IHCs.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to previous work (Yang et al., 2016) showing expression levels in the organ of Corti.

claim: CaBP1 is highly abundant in inner hair cells (IHCs).
source: Besides CaBP2, the structurally related CaBP1 is highly abundant in the IHCs.
evidence: The statement is supported by citation to previous work showing expression levels.

claim: Mutations in the CABP2 gene underlie non-syndromic autosomal recessive hearing loss DFNB93.
source: Mutations in the CABP2 gene underlie non-syndromic autosomal recessive hearing loss DFNB93.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies (Picher, 2017; Koohiyan, 2019; Schrauwen et al., 2012; Sheyanth et al., 2021; Tabatabaiefar et al., 2011).

claim: In Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice, CaV1.3 inactivation is strongly enhanced.
source: In Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice, we find strongly enhanced CaV1.3 inactivation, slowed recovery from inactivation and impaired sustained exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: In Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice, recovery from inactivation is slowed.
source: In Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice, we find strongly enhanced CaV1.3 inactivation, slowed recovery from inactivation and impaired sustained exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from recovery experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: In Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice, sustained exocytosis is impaired.
source: In Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice, we find strongly enhanced CaV1.3 inactivation, slowed recovery from inactivation and impaired sustained exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from capacitance measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mild IHC activation reduces the availability of channels to trigger synaptic transmission in Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice.
source: Already mild IHC activation further reduces the availability of channels to trigger synaptic transmission and may effectively silence synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased inactivation at different holding potentials (Figure 3D, E).

claim: Spontaneous responses of spiral ganglion neurons in vivo are strikingly reduced in Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice.
source: Spontaneous and sound-evoked responses of spiral ganglion neurons in vivo are strikingly reduced and strongly depend on stimulation rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo single-unit recordings shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Sound-evoked responses of spiral ganglion neurons in vivo are strikingly reduced in Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice.
source: Spontaneous and sound-evoked responses of spiral ganglion neurons in vivo are strikingly reduced and strongly depend on stimulation rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo single-unit recordings shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Spiral ganglion neuron responses strongly depend on stimulation rates in Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice.
source: Spontaneous and sound-evoked responses of spiral ganglion neurons in vivo are strikingly reduced and strongly depend on stimulation rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo single-unit recordings at different stimulation rates shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 leads to substantial recovery of IHC synaptic function in Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice.
source: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 leads to substantial recovery of IHC synaptic function and hearing sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings (Figures 1-4) and ABR measurements (Figure 6) in virus-injected animals.

claim: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 leads to substantial recovery of hearing sensitivity in Cabp1/2 double-knockout mice.
source: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 leads to substantial recovery of IHC synaptic function and hearing sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR threshold measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CaBP1 and 2 act together to suppress voltage-dependent inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 channels.
source: We conclude that CaBP1 and 2 act together to suppress voltage- and calcium-dependent inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 channels in order to support sufficient rate of exocytosis and enable fast, temporally precise and indefatigable sound encoding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing enhanced VDI in DKO mice (Figure 2).

claim: CaBP1 and 2 act together to suppress calcium-dependent inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 channels.
source: We conclude that CaBP1 and 2 act together to suppress voltage- and calcium-dependent inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 channels in order to support sufficient rate of exocytosis and enable fast, temporally precise and indefatigable sound encoding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing enhanced CDI in DKO mice (Figure 2).

claim: CaBP1 and 2 enable sufficient rate of exocytosis in IHCs.
source: We conclude that CaBP1 and 2 act together to suppress voltage- and calcium-dependent inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 channels in order to support sufficient rate of exocytosis and enable fast, temporally precise and indefatigable sound encoding.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing impaired exocytosis in DKO mice (Figure 3).

claim: CaBP1 and 2 enable fast sound encoding.
source: We conclude that CaBP1 and 2 act together to suppress voltage- and calcium-dependent inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 channels in order to support sufficient rate of exocytosis and enable fast, temporally precise and indefatigable sound encoding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed impairments in SGN responses (Figure 7) when CaBPs are absent.

claim: CaBP1 and 2 enable temporally precise sound encoding.
source: We conclude that CaBP1 and 2 act together to suppress voltage- and calcium-dependent inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 channels in order to support sufficient rate of exocytosis and enable fast, temporally precise and indefatigable sound encoding.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing increased latency and jitter in DKO SGN responses (Figure 7).

claim: CaBP1 and 2 enable indefatigable sound encoding.
source: We conclude that CaBP1 and 2 act together to suppress voltage- and calcium-dependent inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 channels in order to support sufficient rate of exocytosis and enable fast, temporally precise and indefatigable sound encoding.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing strong adaptation and rate-dependent responses in DKO SGNs (Figure 7).

claim: Calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels is a pivotal initiator of neurotransmission.
source: Calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels (CaVs) is a pivotal initiator of neurotransmission.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about synaptic transmission.

claim: Voltage-gated calcium channels typically undergo considerable Ca2+- and voltage-dependent inactivation.
source: These channels typically undergo considerable Ca2+- and voltage-dependent inactivation (CDI and VDI), which limits the amount of incoming Ca2+ ions and thus possible excitotoxicity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about calcium channel biophysics.

claim: In sensory inner hair cells, the extent of calcium channel inactivation is significantly reduced.
source: In sensory receptor cells such as sensory inner hair cells (IHCs) and photoreceptors, however, the extent of inactivation is significantly reduced to allow encoding of graded and sustained membrane potential fluctuations in response to ongoing sound or visual (t.i. 'darkness') stimuli (reviewed in Pangrsic et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article (Pangrsic et al., 2018).

claim: In photoreceptors, the extent of calcium channel inactivation is significantly reduced.
source: In sensory receptor cells such as sensory inner hair cells (IHCs) and photoreceptors, however, the extent of inactivation is significantly reduced to allow encoding of graded and sustained membrane potential fluctuations in response to ongoing sound or visual (t.i. 'darkness') stimuli (reviewed in Pangrsic et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article (Pangrsic et al., 2018).

claim: Slowed inactivation of L-type CaVs was reported at ribbon synapses of retinal bipolar cells.
source: Furthermore, slowed inactivation of L-type CaVs was also reported at ribbon synapses of retinal bipolar cells (von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1996), which transmit visual information via continuous exocytosis of synaptic vesicles onto retinal ganglion cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1996.

claim: The attenuation of channel inactivation may be largely attributed to the action of calcium-binding proteins, CaBPs.
source: The attenuation of channel inactivation may be largely attributed to the action of calcium-binding proteins, CaBPs (Haeseleer et al., 2000), which primarily abate the calmodulin (CaM)-mediated CDI of CaV channels (Haeseleer et al., 2000; Findeisen and Minor, 2010; Haeseleer et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on CaBP function.

claim: CaBPs primarily abate the calmodulin-mediated CDI of CaV channels.
source: The attenuation of channel inactivation may be largely attributed to the action of calcium-binding proteins, CaBPs (Haeseleer et al., 2000), which primarily abate the calmodulin (CaM)-mediated CDI of CaV channels (Haeseleer et al., 2000; Findeisen and Minor, 2010; Haeseleer et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on CaBP-CaM interactions.

claim: At IHC ribbon synapses, the Ca2+ current is carried through L-type CaV1.3 channels.
source: At the IHC ribbon synapses, the Ca2+ current is carried through the L-type CaV1.3 channels (Baig et al., 2011; Platzer et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baig et al., 2011 and Platzer et al., 2000.

claim: CaV1.3 channel biophysical properties may be regulated by several CaBP family members.
source: Their biophysical properties may be regulated by several CaBP family members (Cui et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2018), but most prominently by CaBP2 (Picher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2007 and Yang et al., 2018.

claim: CaV1.3 channel biophysical properties are most prominently regulated by CaBP2.
source: Their biophysical properties may be regulated by several CaBP family members (Cui et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2018), but most prominently by CaBP2 (Picher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Picher, 2017.

claim: The loss of CaBP2 significantly affects VDI but not CDI of IHC Ca2+ currents.
source: Interestingly, the loss of CaBP2 seems to significantly affect VDI, but not CDI of the IHC Ca2+ currents (Picher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Picher, 2017.

claim: Isolated disruption of CaBP1 in mice leads to at most modest enhancement of IHC CaV1.3 inactivation.
source: Furthermore, isolated disruption of CaBP1 or CaBP4 in mice leads to at most modest enhancement of IHC CaV1.3 inactivation (Cui et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2007 and Yang et al., 2018.

claim: Isolated disruption of CaBP4 in mice leads to at most modest enhancement of IHC CaV1.3 inactivation.
source: Furthermore, isolated disruption of CaBP1 or CaBP4 in mice leads to at most modest enhancement of IHC CaV1.3 inactivation (Cui et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2007 and Yang et al., 2018.

claim: The automodulatory C-terminal domain of the long CaV1.3 isoform is abundant at IHC ribbon synapses.
source: Moreover, the automodulatory C-terminal domain of the long CaV1.3 isoform, abundant at the IHC ribbon synapses (Bock et al., 2011; Scharinger et al., 2015), does not seem critical for CDI suppression either, as its disruption does not lead to hearing impairment (Scharinger et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bock et al., 2011 and Scharinger et al., 2015.

claim: The automodulatory C-terminal domain of the long CaV1.3 isoform does not seem critical for CDI suppression.
source: Moreover, the automodulatory C-terminal domain of the long CaV1.3 isoform, abundant at the IHC ribbon synapses (Bock et al., 2011; Scharinger et al., 2015), does not seem critical for CDI suppression either, as its disruption does not lead to hearing impairment (Scharinger et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Scharinger et al., 2015.

claim: CaBP2 is the most abundant member of the CaBP family in the cochlea.
source: Since CaBP2, followed by the structurally similar CaBP1, are the most abundant members of the CaBP family in the cochlea (Yang et al., 2016), we set out to investigate the phenotype of Cabp1/2 double-knockout (DKO) animals at the systems and cellular levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2016.

claim: CaBP1 is the second most abundant member of the CaBP family in the cochlea.
source: Since CaBP2, followed by the structurally similar CaBP1, are the most abundant members of the CaBP family in the cochlea (Yang et al., 2016), we set out to investigate the phenotype of Cabp1/2 double-knockout (DKO) animals at the systems and cellular levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2016.

claim: Severe hearing impairment was observed in Cabp1/2 double-knockout animals.
source: Severe hearing impairment that we observed in these animals reveals that CaBP1 and 2 act together to attenuate the inactivation of the IHC CaV1.3 channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 almost abolishes sustained exocytosis.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 almost abolishes sustained, and, upon increased hair cell synaptic activity, the fast component of exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Upon increased hair cell synaptic activity, the combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 almost abolishes the fast component of exocytosis.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 almost abolishes sustained, and, upon increased hair cell synaptic activity, the fast component of exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements at different holding potentials shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Such exocytosis defect was not observed in Cabp1 single KO animals.
source: Such phenotype was observed neither in Cabp1 nor in Cabp2 single KO animals (Yang et al., 2018; Picher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: Such exocytosis defect was not observed in Cabp2 single KO animals.
source: Such phenotype was observed neither in Cabp1 nor in Cabp2 single KO animals (Yang et al., 2018; Picher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Picher, 2017.

claim: Viral delivery of Cabp2 coding sequence resulted in substantial recovery of hearing in Cabp1/2 double-knockout animals.
source: These experiments revealed a substantial recovery of hearing, which may be related to the successful restoration of Ca2+ currents and IHC exocytosis upon transgenic expression of CaBP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 restored Ca2+ currents in Cabp1/2 double-knockout IHCs.
source: These experiments revealed a substantial recovery of hearing, which may be related to the successful restoration of Ca2+ currents and IHC exocytosis upon transgenic expression of CaBP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 restored IHC exocytosis in Cabp1/2 double-knockout animals.
source: These experiments revealed a substantial recovery of hearing, which may be related to the successful restoration of Ca2+ currents and IHC exocytosis upon transgenic expression of CaBP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: The functions of CaBP1 and 2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse.
source: Our findings indicate that the functions of CaBP1 and 2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that single knockouts have milder phenotypes than the double knockout.

claim: CaBP1 and 2 together provide sufficient attenuation of channel inactivation to sustain Ca2+ currents required for temporally precise, indefatigable neurotransmission at IHC synapses.
source: Together, they provide sufficient attenuation of channel inactivation to sustain Ca2+ currents and exocytosis required for temporally precise, indefatigable neurotransmission at this synapse.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data from patch-clamp recordings and in vivo SGN recordings.

claim: Peak normalized Ca2+ currents after a 500-ms depolarization show pronounced inactivation in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs compared to WT.
source: Peak normalized Ca2+ currents after a 500-ms depolarization step to the maximum current potential in the apical IHCs of WT and Cabp1/2-DKO animals. Note a pronounced inactivation of the Ca2+ current in the absence of CaBP1 and 2 and partial recovery upon Cabp2 gene replacement.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cabp2 gene replacement leads to partial recovery of Ca2+ current inactivation in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs.
source: Peak normalized Ca2+ currents after a 500-ms depolarization step to the maximum current potential in the apical IHCs of WT and Cabp1/2-DKO animals. Note a pronounced inactivation of the Ca2+ current in the absence of CaBP1 and 2 and partial recovery upon Cabp2 gene replacement.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The fraction of remaining Ca2+ current after 500-ms depolarization is significantly lower in Cabp1/2-DKO compared to WT, Cabp1-KO, and Cabp2-KO.
source: The fraction of the remaining Ca2+ current after a 500-ms depolarization step is depicted for different mouse models acquired at comparable conditions (room temperature, 2 mM extracellular [Ca2+]). The histogram combines the results of this study (Cabp1/2-DKO) with previously published data on CaBP1 (Yang et al., 2018) and CaBP2 (Picher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C comparing different genotypes.

claim: Ca2+ currents are reduced upon a train of 10-ms long depolarization steps in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs.
source: Ca2+ currents upon a train of 10-ms long depolarization steps normalized to the amplitude of the first pulse.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Ca2+-current amplitudes are slightly reduced in IHCs of Cabp1/2-DKO animals transduced with PHP.eB-Cabp2.
source: Ca2+-current–voltage relationships show slightly reduced amplitudes in the IHCs of the Cabp1/2-DKO animals transduced with the PHP.eB-Cabp2.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There is a significant difference in the half-voltage activation (V0.5) between CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs and controls (p < 0.0001).
source: Note a significant difference (asterisks,p < 0.0001, Student's t-test) in the half-voltage activation (V0.5) and slope in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs and the persistence of the voltage shift upon re-expression of CaBP2 (inserts).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of activation curves shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There is a significant difference in the slope of activation curves between CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs and controls (p < 0.0001).
source: Note a significant difference (asterisks,p < 0.0001, Student's t-test) in the half-voltage activation (V0.5) and slope in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs and the persistence of the voltage shift upon re-expression of CaBP2 (inserts).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of activation curves shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The voltage shift in activation persists upon re-expression of CaBP2 in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs.
source: Note a significant difference (asterisks,p < 0.0001, Student's t-test) in the half-voltage activation (V0.5) and slope in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs and the persistence of the voltage shift upon re-expression of CaBP2 (inserts).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: VDI is significantly enhanced in IHCs of Cabp1/2-DKO animals (p < 0.0001).
source: VDI and CDI were both significantly enhanced in the IHCs of Cabp1/2-DKO animals (asterisks; Student's t-test, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CDI is significantly enhanced in IHCs of Cabp1/2-DKO animals (p < 0.0001).
source: VDI and CDI were both significantly enhanced in the IHCs of Cabp1/2-DKO animals (asterisks; Student's t-test, p < 0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VDI in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs is approximately two times larger than in WT IHCs (0.30 ± 0.02 vs 0.13 ± 0.02).
source: The lack of CaBP1 and 2 significantly enhanced both, VDI and CDI of IHC CaV1.3 channels, which were approx. two and six times larger than those in WT IHCs (Figure 2B; VDI: 0.30 ± 0.02 vs 0.13 ± 0.02 and CDI: 0.65 ± 0.01 vs 0.11 ± 0.02 in Cabp1/2 DKO and WT IHCs, respectively; p < 0.0001, Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: CDI in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs is approximately six times larger than in WT IHCs (0.65 ± 0.01 vs 0.11 ± 0.02).
source: The lack of CaBP1 and 2 significantly enhanced both, VDI and CDI of IHC CaV1.3 channels, which were approx. two and six times larger than those in WT IHCs (Figure 2B; VDI: 0.30 ± 0.02 vs 0.13 ± 0.02 and CDI: 0.65 ± 0.01 vs 0.11 ± 0.02 in Cabp1/2 DKO and WT IHCs, respectively; p < 0.0001, Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: In response to short stimuli, capacitance increases were comparable between WT and CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs.

evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Long stimuli evoked significantly smaller capacitance responses in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs compared to WT.
source: In response to short stimuli [primarily recruiting the readily releasable pool (RRP) of vesicles], increases in capacitance were comparable, while long stimuli (reporting sustained exocytosis) evoked significantly smaller responses in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: Peak Ca2+-current amplitudes are comparable between WT and CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs.
source: These results are in line with the observation of comparable peak Ca2+-current amplitudes but reduced calcium charge transfer (QCa) for stimulus durations above 50 ms.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Calcium charge transfer (QCa) is reduced for stimulus durations above 50 ms in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs.
source: These results are in line with the observation of comparable peak Ca2+-current amplitudes but reduced calcium charge transfer (QCa) for stimulus durations above 50 ms.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The reduction in sustained exocytosis cannot completely be explained by the diminished Ca2+ influx in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs.
source: However, calculating exocytosis efficiency revealed that the reduction in sustained exocytosis cannot completely be explained by the diminished Ca2+ influx (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of exocytosis efficiency shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is an additional impairment in exo- or endocytic processes in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs beyond reduced Ca2+ influx.
source: This suggests an additional impairment in exo- or endocytic processes, the underlying mechanism of which is currently unknown.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that exocytosis efficiency is reduced beyond what would be expected from reduced Ca2+ influx.

claim: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 largely restored the efficiency of exocytosis in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs.
source: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 largely restored the efficiency of exocytosis, indicating that the impairment as observed in the IHCs of DKOs is related to the absence of the CaBPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The exocytosis defect observed in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs was not observed in Cabp2-KOs when IHCs are held at hyperpolarized potential at room temperature.
source: Such exocytosis defect was not observed in Cabp2-KOs, suggesting that when IHCs are held at hyperpolarized potential at RT, CaBP1 provides sufficient compensation to obscure the synaptic phenotype (Picher, 2017; Oestreicher et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Picher, 2017 and Oestreicher et al., 2021.

claim: CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs showed significant impairment of sustained exocytosis (p < 0.05 for 20 ms, and <0.001 for 100- and 200-ms step) compared to WT controls.
source: CaBP1/2-deficient inner hair cells (IHCs) showed significant impairment of the sustained exocytosis (p < 0.05 for 20 ms, and <0.001 for 100- and 200-ms step, respectively) and reduced cumulative Ca2+ influx (p < 0.005 for the longest two pulses) as compared to WT controls (black asterisks).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs showed reduced cumulative Ca2+ influx (p < 0.005 for the longest two pulses) compared to WT controls.
source: CaBP1/2-deficient inner hair cells (IHCs) showed significant impairment of the sustained exocytosis (p < 0.05 for 20 ms, and <0.001 for 100- and 200-ms step, respectively) and reduced cumulative Ca2+ influx (p < 0.005 for the longest two pulses) as compared to WT controls (black asterisks).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AAV-mediated delivery of Cabp2 improved IHC synaptic function as compared to non-injected Cabp1/2-DKO controls (p < 0.01 for ΔCm upon 100- and 200-ms step, and p < 0.05 for QCa upon 200-ms step).
source: AAV-mediated delivery of Cabp2 improved IHC synaptic function as compared to non-injected Cabp1/2-DKO controls (p < 0.01 for ΔCm upon 100- and 200-ms step, and p < 0.05 for QCa upon 200-ms step; green asterisks).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is a reduced efficiency of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (p < 0.005 for the two longest test pulses).

evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Intracochlear delivery of PHP.eB-Cabp2 efficiently rescues the reduced efficiency of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis (p < 0.01 and 0.05 for 100- and 200-ms pulse, respectively).
source: Note a reduced efficiency of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis (p < 0.005 for the two longest test pulses; black asterisks), which can be efficiently rescued by intracochlear delivery of PHP.eB-Cabp2 (p < 0.01 and 0.05 for 100- and 200-ms pulse, respectively; green asterisks).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Capacitance measurements at a holding potential of –55 mV reveal an aggravation of the phenotype by additional activation of calcium channels between test pulses.
source: Capacitance measurements at a holding potential of –55 mV reveal an aggravation of the phenotype by additional activation of calcium channels between the test pulses (p < 0.01 for 50 ms, and p < 0.005 for 20-, 100-, and 200-ms pulse) and a further discrepancy between the QCa of WT and CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (2–10 ms: p < 0.05; 20–200 ms: p < 0.001).

claim: At –55 mV holding potential, there is a further discrepancy between the QCa of WT and CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (2–10 ms: p < 0.05; 20–200 ms: p < 0.001).
source: Capacitance measurements at a holding potential of –55 mV reveal an aggravation of the phenotype by additional activation of calcium channels between the test pulses (p < 0.01 for 50 ms, and p < 0.005 for 20-, 100-, and 200-ms pulse) and a further discrepancy between the QCa of WT and CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (2–10 ms: p < 0.05; 20–200 ms: p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: IHCs from Cabp2-injected Cabp1/2-DKO animals showed increased QCa (20–200 ms: p < 0.05) compared to non-injected controls at –55 mV holding potential.
source: Also in these recording conditions, the IHCs from Cabp2-injected Cabp1/2-DKO animals showed increased QCa (20–200 ms: p < 0.05) and exocytosis (100–200 ms: p < 0.005) as compared to non-injected controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: IHCs from Cabp2-injected Cabp1/2-DKO animals showed increased exocytosis (100–200 ms: p < 0.005) compared to non-injected controls at –55 mV holding potential.
source: Also in these recording conditions, the IHCs from Cabp2-injected Cabp1/2-DKO animals showed increased QCa (20–200 ms: p < 0.05) and exocytosis (100–200 ms: p < 0.005) as compared to non-injected controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Raising the holding voltage to –55 mV resulted in a 60 ± 4% reduction in maximal Ca2+ currents in DKO IHCs.

evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experiments shown in Figure 3D, E.

claim: Raising the holding voltage to –55 mV resulted in a 25 ± 4% reduction in maximal Ca2+ currents in WT IHCs.

evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experiments shown in Figure 3D, E.

claim: At –55 mV holding potential, there was a complete loss of sustained exocytosis in DKO IHCs (p < 0.005).
source: Consequently, further discrepancy between the QCa in IHCs of WT and DKO animals was observed (p < 0.001), which in DKO animals resulted in a complete loss of sustained exocytosis (Figure 3D; p < 0.005).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tone bursts up to 90 dB SPL barely elicited any ABR response in young Cabp1/2-DKO animals.

claim: The absence of ABR wave I suggests reduced and/or desynchronized spiking of spiral ganglion neurons.

claim: CaBP2 is absent from SGNs.
source: Since Cabp1 KO animals show normal hearing several weeks after birth, and CaBP2 is absent from SGNs, we interpret the hearing impairment of the Cabp1/2 DKO animals to be primarily due to defects of hair cell function and judge contribution by SGN dysfunction as rather unlikely, at least in the early postnatal weeks.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data cited earlier.

claim: The hearing impairment of Cabp1/2 DKO animals is primarily due to defects of hair cell function.
source: Since Cabp1 KO animals show normal hearing several weeks after birth, and CaBP2 is absent from SGNs, we interpret the hearing impairment of the Cabp1/2 DKO animals to be primarily due to defects of hair cell function and judge contribution by SGN dysfunction as rather unlikely, at least in the early postnatal weeks.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on the expression patterns and phenotypes.

claim: ABR thresholds of Cabp1 KO animals are normal at 4 weeks of age but deteriorate with age, starting with high-frequency hearing loss at 9 weeks.
source: The ABR thresholds of Cabp1 KO animals are normal at 4 weeks of age, but deteriorate with age, starting with high-frequency hearing loss at 9 weeks.
evidence: The claim is based on previous characterization of Cabp1 KO animals.

claim: Suprathreshold ABRs to tone burst stimulation in Cabp1 KO animals show increased amplitudes and reduced latencies during the first 2 months after birth.
source: Conversely, the suprathreshold ABRs to tone burst stimulation show increased amplitudes and reduced latencies during the first 2 months after birth.
evidence: The claim is based on previous characterization of Cabp1 KO animals.

claim: The increased ABR amplitudes in young Cabp1 KO animals suggested enhanced SGN activity at first, followed by slowly progressing functional decline.
source: This suggested enhanced SGN activity at first, followed by slowly progressing functional decline, possibly due to overexcitability-related toxicity (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation from Yang et al., 2018.

claim: Overexcitability-related effects are not expected to occur in DKO animals due to early strong impairment of hair cell synaptic function.
source: Due to early strong impairment of hair cell synaptic function, the latter effects are not expected to occur in the DKO animals.
evidence: This is the authors' inference based on the DKO phenotype.

claim: ABR thresholds for clicks were further increased in DKO animals at two compared to 1 month of age.
source: However, ABR thresholds for clicks were further increased and an additional reduction in the summating potential was observed in the DKO animals at two as compared to 1 month of age despite relatively well-preserved DPOAEs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: An additional reduction in the summating potential was observed in DKO animals at two compared to 1 month of age.
source: However, ABR thresholds for clicks were further increased and an additional reduction in the summating potential was observed in the DKO animals at two as compared to 1 month of age despite relatively well-preserved DPOAEs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: It remains to be clarified whether the absence of CaBP1 and 2 may affect IHC mechanotransduction at more mature stage.
source: It thus remains to be clarified whether the absence of CaBP1 and 2 may affect (IHC) mechanotransduction at more mature stage.
evidence: This is a question raised by the authors for future investigation.

claim: CaBPs share similarities with calcium and integrin-binding protein 2 (CIB2), which is associated with hair bundle defects.
source: Intriguingly, CaBPs share similarities with calcium and integrin-binding protein 2 (CIB2), associated with hair bundle defects (Giese et al., 2017; Riazuddin et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on CIB2.

claim: When CaBP2 was overexpressed in DKO animals, suprathreshold responses of ABR wave I were very large.
source: When we overexpressed CaBP2 in the DKO animals, interestingly, suprathreshold responses of ABR wave I were very large (Figure 6) and the summated wave I–IV responses were not distinguishable from WT responses (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When CaBP2 was overexpressed in DKO animals, the summated wave I–IV responses were not distinguishable from WT responses.
source: When we overexpressed CaBP2 in the DKO animals, interestingly, suprathreshold responses of ABR wave I were very large (Figure 6) and the summated wave I–IV responses were not distinguishable from WT responses (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Tone burst and click thresholds did not completely recover to WT levels upon CaBP2 overexpression in DKO animals.
source: However, tone burst and click thresholds did not completely recover to WT levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR threshold data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The difference in the extent of rescue of threshold and suprathreshold responses may be due to possibly distinct requirements for CaBPs at synapses providing inputs to low- or high-threshold SGN fibers.
source: The difference in the extent of rescue of threshold and suprathreshold responses may be due to possibly distinct requirements for CaBPs at synapses providing inputs to low- or high-threshold SGN fibers.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the partial rescue.

claim: Not much is known about possible differences in CaV1.3 properties and interaction partners at distinct ribbons.
source: Apart from a small shift in voltage activation and abundance of the channels (Ohn et al., 2016), not much is known about the possible differences in the CaV1.3 properties and interaction partners at distinct ribbons.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: It is not known whether the composition of the channel complex differs systematically between ribbon-AZs partnered by different classes of SGN fibers.
source: Neither is it known whether the composition of the channel complex t.i. proportions of alpha subunit splice variants (Scharinger et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2008; Vincent et al., 2017), and different beta subunits (Ortner et al., 2020) differs systematically between ribbon-AZs partnered by different classes of SGN fibers.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: Different amounts of rescue of threshold vs suprathreshold responses could be due to confounding effects of CaBP1 and 2.
source: Different amounts of rescue of threshold vs suprathreshold responses could be further due to confounding effects of CaBP1 and 2, for example augmented SGN response in Cabp2-injected DKO animals still lacking CaBP1 (reminiscent of the phenotype of young Cabp1 KOs) in combination with 'only' partial rescue of CaBP2 function.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the partial rescue.

claim: Possible adverse effects of exogenous expression of CaBP2 include off-target toxicity and uncontrolled overexpression of the transgene.
source: Possible adverse effects of exogenous expression of CaBP2, for example off-target toxicity and uncontrolled overexpression of the transgene, have been discussed previously (Oestreicher et al., 2021), and further experiments need to be performed in the future to achieve (close to) complete rescue of hearing function in these mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Oestreicher et al., 2021.

claim: The amount of CaV1.3 inactivation increases dramatically when IHCs lack both major CaBPs.
source: Our results reveal that the amount of CaV1.3 inactivation increases dramatically when IHCs lack both major CaBPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The sole loss of either CaBP1 or 2 can be largely compensated by the other of the two CaBP members.
source: This suggests that the sole loss of either CaBP1 or 2, can be largely compensated by the other of the two CaBP members.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of single and double knockout phenotypes.

claim: The loss of CaBP2 alone results in progressive hearing impairment in mice and DFNB93 in humans.
source: Yet, the loss of CaBP2 alone still results in progressive hearing impairment in mice and DFNB93 in humans.
evidence: The claim is supported by previous studies on Cabp2 KO mice and human patients.

claim: The inability of CaBP1 to fully replace CaBP2 in CaBP2-deficient IHCs may stem from either too low concentration of CaBP1 or from distinct properties of the two proteins.
source: The inability of CaBP1 to fully replace CaBP2 in the CaBP2-deficient IHCs may stem from either too low concentration of CaBP1 (and other CaBPs), or from distinct properties of the two proteins (enabling CaBP2 to exert more potent suppression of CaV1.3 inactivation, e.g. VDI, or potentially performing additional, yet unidentified cellular function).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the incomplete compensation.

claim: Even the overexpression of CaBP2 did not completely rescue the hearing phenotype of DKO animals.
source: Interestingly, even the overexpression of CaBP2 did not completely rescue the hearing phenotype of DKO animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Future experiments involving overexpression of CaBP1 in Cabp2 SKO and/or Cabp1/2 DKO animals are required to gain better understanding of potentially distinct functions of the two major CaBPs.
source: Future experiments involving overexpression of CaBP1 (and possibly CaBP1-2 molecular chimeras) in Cabp2 SKO and/or Cabp1/2 DKO animals together with further biophysical interaction studies are required to gain a better understanding of the potentially distinct functions performed by the two major CaBPs in the hair cells.
evidence: This is a proposal for future research directions.

claim: Patch-clamp recordings revealed normal whole-cell exocytosis in CaBP2-deficient IHCs despite enhanced inactivation of calcium channels.
source: Previously, patch-clamp recordings surprisingly revealed normal whole-cell exocytosis in CaBP2-deficient IHCs despite enhanced inactivation of calcium channels (Picher, 2017), and no obvious defects in the CaBP1-deficient IHCs (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Picher, 2017 and Yang et al., 2018.

claim: No obvious defects were observed in CaBP1-deficient IHCs in previous patch-clamp recordings.
source: Previously, patch-clamp recordings surprisingly revealed normal whole-cell exocytosis in CaBP2-deficient IHCs despite enhanced inactivation of calcium channels (Picher, 2017), and no obvious defects in the CaBP1-deficient IHCs (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: IHCs deficient in both CaBP1 and 2 displayed strongly impaired exocytosis.
source: In contrast, IHCs deficient in both, CaBP1 and 2, displayed strongly impaired exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of CaBP2 in IHCs resulted in partial recovery of Ca2+ influx.
source: Transgenic overexpression of CaBP2 in IHCs resulted in a partial recovery of the Ca2+ influx and an even better recovery of exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of CaBP2 in IHCs resulted in even better recovery of exocytosis than Ca2+ influx.
source: Transgenic overexpression of CaBP2 in IHCs resulted in a partial recovery of the Ca2+ influx and an even better recovery of exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: These results corroborate the hypothesis of the role of CaBPs in preventing extensive steady-state inactivation of CaV1.3 channels to support sufficient synaptic exocytosis for proper sound encoding.
source: Together, these results corroborate the hypothesis of the role of CaBPs in preventing extensive steady-state inactivation of CaV1.3 channels to support sufficient synaptic exocytosis for proper sound encoding (Picher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data from the study and citation to Picher, 2017.

claim: The lack of CaBP1 and 2 seems to impair sustained exocytosis and efficiency of exocytosis beyond the levels that could be attributed to reduced QCa.
source: The lack of CaBP1 and 2 seems to impair sustained exocytosis and efficiency of exocytosis beyond the levels that could be attributed to reduced QCa.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: It is not clear how CaBPs may directly affect exocytosis, for example by influencing the coupling of CaV1.3 channels and synaptic vesicles.
source: At present, it is not clear how CaBPs may directly affect the exocytosis, for example by influencing the coupling of the CaV1.3 channels and synaptic vesicles or potentially affecting the expression levels of other synaptic proteins that mediate synaptic vesicle replenishment.
evidence: This is a statement about current gaps in understanding.

claim: CaBP1 and 2 have been reported to modulate CaMKII activity.
source: In this respect, it is worth noting that CaBP1 and 2 have been reported to modulate CaMKII activity (Haeseleer et al., 2000), which in turn may through phosphorylation modify the Ca2+ affinity of otoferlin C2 domains (Meese et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haeseleer et al., 2000 and Meese et al., 2017.

claim: CaMKII may through phosphorylation modify the Ca2+ affinity of otoferlin C2 domains.
source: In this respect, it is worth noting that CaBP1 and 2 have been reported to modulate CaMKII activity (Haeseleer et al., 2000), which in turn may through phosphorylation modify the Ca2+ affinity of otoferlin C2 domains (Meese et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Meese et al., 2017.

claim: It is essential to investigate if CaBPs regulate the function of otoferlin and thus synaptic processes.
source: In the future, it is thus essential to investigate if CaBPs regulate the function of otoferlin and thus synaptic processes.
evidence: This is a proposal for future research.

claim: CaM has been suggested to be involved in endocytosis.
source: Furthermore, other members of the CaBP/CaM family have been suggested to interact with synaptic proteins and/or be involved in the regulation of synaptic vesicle cycle: CaM in endocytosis (Wu et al., 2009), CaBP5 in priming via interaction with Munc18-1 (Sokal and Haeseleer, 2011), CaBP1 via inhibition of IP3 receptors (Haynes et al., 2004; Kasri et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2009.

claim: CaBP5 has been suggested to be involved in priming via interaction with Munc18-1.
source: Furthermore, other members of the CaBP/CaM family have been suggested to interact with synaptic proteins and/or be involved in the regulation of synaptic vesicle cycle: CaM in endocytosis (Wu et al., 2009), CaBP5 in priming via interaction with Munc18-1 (Sokal and Haeseleer, 2011), CaBP1 via inhibition of IP3 receptors (Haynes et al., 2004; Kasri et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sokal and Haeseleer, 2011.

claim: CaBP1 has been suggested to be involved in synaptic vesicle cycle via inhibition of IP3 receptors.
source: Furthermore, other members of the CaBP/CaM family have been suggested to interact with synaptic proteins and/or be involved in the regulation of synaptic vesicle cycle: CaM in endocytosis (Wu et al., 2009), CaBP5 in priming via interaction with Munc18-1 (Sokal and Haeseleer, 2011), CaBP1 via inhibition of IP3 receptors (Haynes et al., 2004; Kasri et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haynes et al., 2004 and Kasri et al., 2004.

claim: An important challenge for future studies is to identify further CaBP(2)-interaction partners and possible functions beyond modulation of calcium channels.
source: An important challenge for future studies is to identify further CaBP(2)-interaction partners and possible functions beyond modulation of calcium channels.
evidence: This is a proposal for future research directions.

claim: CaBPs speed-up recovery of CaV1.3 channels from inactivation after prolonged milder stimulation.
source: In the IHCs of injected DKO animals, this second component appeared smaller and faster, suggesting that CaBPs speed-up recovery of CaV1.3 channels from inactivation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the recovery kinetics data shown in Figure 4C and Table 1.

claim: Fast recovery of CaV1.3 from inactivation after 500-ms depolarization in DKO IHCs may be due to faster Ca2+ clearance.
source: We hypothesize this to be due to faster Ca2+ clearance from the DKO IHC synapses as the intracellular [Ca2+] levels are expected to rise significantly less in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs due to fast and pronounced CaV1.3 inactivation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the recovery kinetics.

claim: Higher [Ca2+] may buildup at the synapses of WT and 'rescued' DKO IHCs, consequently prolonging CDI.
source: In contrast, higher [Ca2+] may buildup at the synapses of WT and 'rescued' DKO IHCs; consequently, CDI may be prolonged.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the recovery kinetics.

claim: CaBP2 may act as a slow mobile calcium buffer.
source: Another plausible explanation for the observation is, if we consider that CaPB2 may act as a slow mobile calcium buffer (Picher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Picher, 2017.

claim: In the presence of excessive 'overexpressed' CaBP2, depolarization-evoked intracellular [Ca2+] transients may become biexponential.
source: In the presence of excessive 'overexpressed' CaBP2 in injected IHCs of DKO animals, the depolarization-evoked intracellular [Ca2+] transients may become biexponential as has been described for parvalbumin alpha (Lee et al., 2000), which may prolong the time constant of Ca2+ clearance and determine the kinetics of channel recovery from inactivation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by citation to Lee et al., 2000.

claim: Results of recovery upon 500-ms depolarization may mostly reflect the kinetics of Ca2+ clearance from the cytosol.
source: Our results of the recovery upon 500-ms depolarization may thus mostly reflect the kinetics of the Ca2+ clearance from the cytosol, while the experiments with prolonged sine wave stimulation (when e.g. the function of calcium pumps and other extrusion systems and intracellular [Ca2+] levels may be at equilibrium), may report the speed of calcium channel recovery from a slow inactivation.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their recovery experiments.

claim: Experiments with prolonged sine wave stimulation may report the speed of calcium channel recovery from slow inactivation.
source: Our results of the recovery upon 500-ms depolarization may thus mostly reflect the kinetics of the Ca2+ clearance from the cytosol, while the experiments with prolonged sine wave stimulation (when e.g. the function of calcium pumps and other extrusion systems and intracellular [Ca2+] levels may be at equilibrium), may report the speed of calcium channel recovery from a slow inactivation.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their recovery experiments.

claim: Slow inactivation with very slow recovery was described for NaV, KV, and CaV channels.
source: Slow inactivation with very slow recovery was described for NaV, KV, and CaV channels (Bezanilla et al., 1982; Payandeh et al., 2012; Olcese et al., 1997; Ferreira et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on channel inactivation.

claim: The time constant of recovery of CaV1.2 from slow VDI was comparably shorter (4 s) than observed in the present study.
source: It has to be noted that the time constant of recovery of CaV1.2 from slow VDI was comparably shorter (4 s) as observed in the present study (Ferreira et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ferreira et al., 2003.

claim: Future experiments combining patch-clamp recordings with calcium imaging should be employed to address questions about recovery kinetics.
source: Future experiments combining patch-clamp recordings with calcium imaging should be employed to address this question further.
evidence: This is a proposal for future research.

claim: From in vitro recordings at higher holding potential, we predict that in vivo a noteworthy proportion of CaV1.3 channels may be effectively inactivated.
source: From our in vitro recordings at higher holding potential or upon prolonged stimulation with small voltage oscillations we predict that in vivo a noteworthy proportion of CaV1.3 channels may be effectively inactivated and not available for mediating IHC synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a prediction based on in vitro data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Effectively inactivated CaV1.3 channels could explain the low experimental yield and low spontaneous spiking rates of SGNs in DKO animals.
source: This could explain the low experimental yield, the low 'spontaneous' spiking rates of the SGNs and lower sound-evoked spike rates with higher thresholds.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation connecting in vitro and in vivo findings.

claim: Thresholds may be high for tone bursts in ABR measurements due to high proportion of inactivated channels upon stimuli at high repetition rate.
source: Similarly, thresholds may be high for tone bursts in the ABR measurements due to high proportion of inactivated channels upon stimuli at high repetition rate used for these recordings (20–40 Hz repetition rate for click and tone burst stimulation, respectively).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the ABR data.

claim: Any sound stimulation and potentially even spontaneous activity may effectively silence DKO synapses.
source: We believe that any sound stimulation and potentially even spontaneous activity may effectively silence DKO synapses.
evidence: This is the authors' hypothesis based on the combined data.

claim: Longer interstimulus intervals allow a larger proportion of channels to recover between stimuli, increasing onset rates of SGN spiking while decreasing first spike latency and jitter.
source: As expected, longer interstimulus intervals may allow a larger proportion of channels to recover between stimuli, increasing the onset rates of SGN spiking while decreasing the first spike latency and jitter.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: High-intensity stimulation had to be used in DKO animals to evoke an increase in SGN spiking.
source: Still, high-intensity stimulation had to be used in the DKO animals to evoke an increase in SGN spiking.
evidence: This describes the experimental observations from single-unit recordings.

claim: It is possible that spontaneous activity and/or routines used to determine SGN characteristic frequency inactivate a majority of IHC CaV1.3 channels.
source: It is possible that spontaneous activity and/or our routines used to determine the SGN characteristic frequency inactivate a majority of IHC CaV1.3 channels thus not allowing reliable assessment of the characteristic frequency.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain experimental difficulties.

claim: In addition to CaV1.3 channel inactivation, other factors may contribute to low hearing sensitivity, such as possible impairment of synaptic vesicle replenishment or IHC mechanotransduction.
source: In addition to CaV1.3 channel inactivation, other factors may contribute to low hearing sensitivity, such as possible impairment of synaptic vesicle replenishment, or IHC mechanotransduction, and, in some cases, impaired cochlear amplification.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential contributing factors to the phenotype.

claim: A complete lack of BK channels was shown to affect IHC resting potential, receptor potential amplitude and timing, and consequently the timing and frequency of spiking in SGNs.
source: A complete lack of BK channels was shown to affect the IHC resting potential, receptor potential amplitude and timing, and consequently the timing and frequency of spiking in the SGNs (Oliver et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Oliver et al., 2006.

claim: Lower expression of BK channels is not expected to significantly affect hearing thresholds, at least initially.
source: Lower expression of BK channels is not expected to significantly affect hearing thresholds, at least initially (Rüttiger et al., 2004; Maison et al., 2013; Pyott et al., 2007), and thus likely does not contribute to the hearing defect of the Cabp1/2 DKO animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on BK channel function.

claim: At advanced ages, the effects of reduced BK expression may combine with the lack of CaBPs to additionally desynchronize already scarce spikes in auditory nerve fibers.
source: However, at advanced ages, the effects described above may combine with the lack of CaBPs to additionally desynchronize already scarce spikes in the auditory nerve fibers.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about potential age-related effects.

claim: The SGN sound encoding phenotype in Cabp2-KO mice was surprisingly mild compared to the deficits observed in DFNB93 patients.
source: The SGN sound encoding phenotype in Cabp2-KO mice was surprisingly mild compared to the deficits observed in DFNB93 patients (Picher, 2017; Schrauwen et al., 2012): SGN thresholds and evoked spike rates were only minimally affected (Picher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Picher, 2017 and Schrauwen et al., 2012.

claim: SGN thresholds and evoked spike rates were only minimally affected in Cabp2-KO mice.
source: The SGN sound encoding phenotype in Cabp2-KO mice was surprisingly mild compared to the deficits observed in DFNB93 patients (Picher, 2017; Schrauwen et al., 2012): SGN thresholds and evoked spike rates were only minimally affected (Picher, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Picher, 2017.

claim: Synaptic activity in response to everyday sounds could inactivate calcium channels and reduce SGN spiking in DFNB93 patients.
source: Given the strong recovery phenotype in the DKO we now consider the possibility that synaptic activity in response to everyday sounds could already inactivate calcium channels and reduce SGN spiking.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the DKO phenotype.

claim: Communication in daily life would be more strongly impaired than audiometric data obtained in a soundproof chamber in DFNB93 patients.
source: In this case, communication in daily life would be more strongly impaired than audiometric data obtained in a soundproof chamber, especially when short stimuli separated by silent intervals are used.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the authors' hypothesis about channel inactivation.

claim: In mild cases of DFNB93, a gap detection test may be used to assess auditory fatigue.
source: In mild cases, a gap detection test may be used to assess auditory fatigue.
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Patients with stronger channel inactivation phenotype might not benefit much from sound amplification by hearing aids.
source: Based on our data, we further predict that patients that have a stronger channel inactivation phenotype might not benefit much from sound amplification by hearing aids.
evidence: This is a clinical prediction based on the study findings.

claim: DFNB93 patients should use technologies that improve signal to noise ratio such as noise cancellation, directional microphones, and wireless transmitters.
source: Instead, they should use technologies that improve the signal to noise ratio (e.g. noise cancellation, directional microphones, and wireless transmitters).
evidence: This is a clinical recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Gene therapy may be an alternative or additional future treatment approach for DFNB93.
source: An alternative or additional future treatment approach may be gene therapy.
evidence: This is a proposal for future clinical applications.

claim: Re-expression of CaBP2 by genetic treatment partially restored CaV1.3 properties, IHC exocytosis and consequently ABR wave amplitudes and thresholds.
source: In our hands, re-expression of CaBP2 by genetic treatment partially restored CaV1.3 properties, IHC exocytosis and consequently ABR wave amplitudes and thresholds.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1-6.

claim: The successful viral rescue supports the view that reversible inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 currents is the main mechanism of hearing loss in CaBP-related deafness.
source: This successful viral rescue supports the view that a reversible inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 currents is the main mechanism of hearing loss in CaBP-related deafness, which can be targeted by gene therapy in the future.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the rescue experiments.

claim: Reversible inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 currents can be targeted by gene therapy in the future.
source: This successful viral rescue supports the view that a reversible inactivation of IHC CaV1.3 currents is the main mechanism of hearing loss in CaBP-related deafness, which can be targeted by gene therapy in the future.
evidence: This is a proposal for future therapeutic applications based on the study findings.
